pragma solidity ^0.8.20;

/**
 * @dev Interface of the ERC-20 Permit extension allowing approvals to be made via signatures, as defined in
 * https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-2612[ERC-2612].
 *
 * Adds the {permit} method, which can be used to change an account's ERC-20 allowance (see {IERC20-allowance}) by
 * presenting a message signed by the account. By not relying on {IERC20-approve}, the token holder account doesn't
 * need to send a transaction, and thus is not required to hold Ether at all.
 *
 * ==== Security Considerations
 *
 * There are two important considerations concerning the use of `permit`. The first is that a valid permit signature
 * expresses an allowance, and it should not be assumed to convey additional meaning. In particular, it should not be
 * considered as an intention to spend the allowance in any specific way. The second is that because permits have
 * built-in replay protection and can be submitted by anyone, they can be frontrun. A protocol that uses permits should
 * take this into consideration and allow a `permit` call to fail. Combining these two aspects, a pattern that may be
 * generally recommended is:
 *
 * ```solidity
 * function doThingWithPermit(..., uint256 value, uint256 deadline, uint8 v, bytes32 r, bytes32 s) public {
 *     try token.permit(msg.sender, address(this), value, deadline, v, r, s) {} catch {}
 *     doThing(..., value);
 * }
 *
 * function doThing(..., uint256 value) public {
 *     token.safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), value);
 *     ...
 * }
 * ```
 *
 * Observe that: 1) `msg.sender` is used as the owner, leaving no ambiguity as to the signer intent, and 2) the use of
 * `try/catch` allows the permit to fail and makes the code tolerant to frontrunning. (See also
 * {SafeERC20-safeTransferFrom}).
 *
 * Additionally, note that smart contract wallets (such as Argent or Safe) are not able to produce permit signatures, so
 * contracts should have entry points that don't rely on permit.
 */
interface IERC20Permit {
    /**
     * @dev Sets `value` as the allowance of `spender` over ``owner``'s tokens,
     * given ``owner``'s signed approval.
     *
     * IMPORTANT: The same issues {IERC20-approve} has related to transaction
     * ordering also apply here.
     *
     * Emits an {Approval} event.
     *
     * Requirements:
     *
     * - `spender` cannot be the zero address.
     * - `deadline` must be a timestamp in the future.
     * - `v`, `r` and `s` must be a valid `secp256k1` signature from `owner`
     * over the EIP712-formatted function arguments.
     * - the signature must use ``owner``'s current nonce (see {nonces}).
     *
     * For more information on the signature format, see the
     * https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-2612#specification[relevant EIP
     * section].
     *
     * CAUTION: See Security Considerations above.
     */
    function permit(
        address owner,
        address spender,
        uint256 value,
        uint256 deadline,
        uint8 v,
        bytes32 r,
        bytes32 s
    ) external;

    /**
     * @dev Returns the current nonce for `owner`. This value must be
     * included whenever a signature is generated for {permit}.
     *
     * Every successful call to {permit} increases ``owner``'s nonce by one. This
     * prevents a signature from being used multiple times.
     */
    function nonces(address owner) external view returns (uint256);

    /**
     * @dev Returns the domain separator used in the encoding of the signature for {permit}, as defined by {EIP712}.
     */
    // solhint-disable-next-line func-name-mixedcase
    function DOMAIN_SEPARATOR() external view returns (bytes32);
}

# Contract Addresses

Published contract addresses and deployment statuses for Ramses across supported chains.

Source: https://www.ramses.xyz/docs/contract-addresses

Ramses DEX deployments and RAM/r33 OFT routes are separate networks. The OFT table shows token connectivity, while the chain tabs show published deployment-specific contracts. Base is OFT-only among the deployments listed here and therefore has no DEX tab. Arbitrum is DEX-only and has no listed live RAM or r33 OFT route. HyperEVM, Polygon, and Robinhood Chain have both a Ramses DEX deployment and live OFT connectivity.

**r33** is the liquid staked xRAM token, known as **hyperRAM on HyperEVM**. Both names refer to the same product; the tables below identify its contract on each listed network.

## RAM & r33 OFT Network

| Chain | RAM Endpoint | r33 Endpoint | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **HyperEVM** | [Native RAM](https://hyperevmscan.io/address/0x555570a286F15EbDFE42B66eDE2f724Aa1AB5555) · [Adapter](https://hyperevmscan.io/address/0xe1C39b767E968a57aF2Ecad2F5b09eE2E7874D9f) | [Native r33 / hyperRAM](https://hyperevmscan.io/address/0x5555c2542836e7a6c8D3E133D5AA9773b65D5555) · [Adapter](https://hyperevmscan.io/address/0xA4C83170f2A1410681D586a1e8C2E4620a93a081) | Current home; live |
| **Base** | [RAM OFT](https://basescan.org/address/0x03FE4dd36DB2c8483E258974Db82D07d82F8d239) | [r33 OFT](https://basescan.org/address/0xADd32480630A16dfAcEe6eeFcB3ab2181449Dc3B) | Live satellite |
| **Polygon** | [RAM OFT](https://polygonscan.com/address/0x8483F906187c45cC2b491F26dBbDD7C3231597e8) | [r33 OFT](https://polygonscan.com/address/0xe3Bc31a2F12ACFF0e5ffb2b37985fDd913b98B7a) | Live satellite |
| **Robinhood Chain** | [RAM OFT](https://robin.etherscan.io/address/0x5173D45A1191eE33cBB7D8c7e65f21B04eD54802) | [r33 OFT](https://robin.etherscan.io/address/0x4e5195469A0360f5dfe811730C9CCaCFF0a0FeeE) | Live satellite |
| **Ethereum Mainnet** | [Configured RAM endpoint](https://etherscan.io/address/0x95CBe89A7712ad5b99ff2956e9d5369fC65959eb) | [Configured r33 endpoint](https://etherscan.io/address/0x2eBd7B85a4E08D5B508b04BA147976C94afE6590) | Route inactive; eventual hub |

> **DEX and OFT Availability**
>
> Base appears in the OFT table because its RAM and r33 satellite contracts are live, but no Ramses DEX deployment is listed there. Arbitrum appears in the DEX tabs because its Ramses contracts are live, but it is not an active RAM or r33 OFT route. Ethereum has configured OFT endpoints, but the route remains inactive.

warnings: Static deployment/source/ABI metadata only; no persistent runtime attestation, live grants, liquidity, funding, financial safety, route coverage or successful-execution assurance. Independent policies, grants, pauses and canonical calldata/value checks remain mandatory.

This is Ramses current Arbitrum V3 concentrated-liquidity SwapRouter 0x4730e03EB4a58A5e20244062D5f9A99bCf5770a6 published in current primary deployment docs, NOT excluded retired Ramses V1 or the separately labeled Legacy V2 router. No unsupported HyperEVM/Robinhood chain, OFT transfer or token-migration scope is added. The deployed router is nonproxy; full deployment-bound matching source and original ABI are retained.

Only exactInputSingle and exactOutputSingle are admitted. Their tuple supplies tokenIn/tokenOut, signed int24 tickSpacing, recipient, deadline, input/output quantity bound and sqrtPriceLimitX96. These are fixed financial swap parameters, not a caller-selected execution target, selector or arbitrary command. Source computes the pool deterministically using immutable deployer, sorted tokens, tickSpacing and fixed init-code hash; callback verifies sender against that derived pool. Direct callback, multicall, UniversalRouter commands, permits, sweeps and refunds remain excluded.

Current explorer immutable getters identify WETH9=0x82aF49447D8a07e3bd95BD0d56f35241523fBab1 and pool deployer=0xb722efaAbe807FAeA16068f595EaA9aa1a62CECD, matching the current primary registry. Valid token pairs/tick spacing require a deployed supported pool and suitable liquidity. This snapshot does not inventory or attest every pool, token, oracle, factory role or future market configuration.

Caller is fixed as payer. ERC20 input is pulled from msg.sender by router allowance in validated pool callback; no raw pool prefunding or standalone mint/burn is used. For WETH9 input the payment routine first uses any native ETH already held by router, wrapping only amount owed, then otherwise pulls WETH. For ordinary token-funded swaps send zero native value and pre-establish needed input allowance. Catalog adds no approval/signature authority.

Both selected ABI methods are payable but do not automatically refund unused ETH, unwrap WETH output or sweep assets. Native-funded exact-output swaps and nonzero price-limit partial fills can leave ETH/input residue publicly recoverable through excluded refund/sweep methods. Do not overpay, prefund router, set recipient=zero/router, or assume a complete native-asset workflow; route output directly to intended nonzero recipient. Zero recipient deliberately redirects output into router custody. Token output to third parties is intentional recipient authority, not own-wallet protection.

exactInputSingle requests amountIn and enforces amountOut>=amountOutMinimum. A nonzero sqrtPriceLimitX96 can produce a partial input fill. exactOutputSingle enforces amountIn<=amountInMaximum; when sqrtPriceLimitX96=0 source also requires full amountOut, while a nonzero limit explicitly permits receiving less than requested output. Set limits intentionally; return values are respectively output received and input paid. No fee-on-transfer/rebasing-token compatibility or receiver delta guarantee is asserted.

Quantity fields use each token base units, deadline uses Unix seconds with block.timestamp<=deadline, sqrtPriceLimitX96 uses Q64.96, and tickSpacing is NOT a fee basis-point field. Zero price limit selects near-extreme allowed V3 price boundary. Pool swap math determines price impact, rounding and fees; use meaningful minimum-output/maximum-input, deadline and optional directional price bound. No fixed rate or fee is promised.

Current primary docs distinguish V3 AMM from Legacy V2 and identify Arbitrum as DEX-only, separate from token OFT connectivity. This does not restore retired V1 deployments. Packed multihop path methods are separately inventoried but not admitted in this explicitly typed single-pool scope; no claim they are arbitrary executable calldata is made.
